item.title: mRNA Ebola vaccine trial launched in Uganda
item.description: Trials of an experimental Ebola vaccine launched in Uganda on Friday, while a global NGO said it had bought 1.5 million doses of another candidate, as the race heats up to contain the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo strain of Ebola behind the outbreak in DRC, which has caused more than 5,700 confirmed deaths out of more than 11,000 cases since being declared in May, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Two experimental vaccines are due to start testing on Monday in the outbreak’s epicentre in eastern DRC, the WHO said, focusing on contacts of cases and people deemed at high risk of infection. But neighbouring Uganda announced it had also launched a trial of one of the vaccines, developed by the US-based Moderna group using the mRNA technology made famous during the Covid pandemic. The Uganda Virus Research Institute described it as “Africa’s first mRNA Phase I clinical trial”, conducted in collaboration with Moderna. It will test 224 healthy volunteers aged between one and 65 to measure its safety and immunity potential. The other potential vaccine is the ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector vaccine developed by India’s Serum Institute and the University of Oxford — which will also begin testing in DRC on Monday. But Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, which brings together government and private donors to help developing countries acquire jabs at affordable prices, is not waiting around. After the Covid-19 pandemic, the alliance set up a new $50 million First Response Fund — under a so-called “No Regrets” approach — to allow it to buy up doses in advance even before they have been fully tested. – Deployment – Gavi signed a purchase commitment this week with the Serum Institute for 1.5 million doses of the ChAdOx1, and plans to have “hundreds of thousands” ready to deploy should the trials prove successful and they are approved by the WHO and DRC government. “We’re investing in it, hoping that the signals will be positive, and if that is the case, we’ll have gained months and months on the deployment,” Emanuele Capobianco, Gavi’s director of global health security, told AFP. He said he hoped for trials to conclude “within the first half of 2027” and even “within the first quarter” in a more optimistic scenario. Gavi also has a stockpile of 500,000 doses of an existing vaccine, Ervebo, used against the Zaire strain of Ebola, which began testing last month to see if it is also effective against Bundibugyo. Despite a long and porous border with eastern DRC, Uganda has successfully contained the virus after receiving some imported cases earlier this year. It was declared Ebola-free in August after registering 20 cases, including two deaths. The post mRNA Ebola vaccine trial launched in Uganda appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Nigeria set to bid to host maiden U-17 WAFCON
item.description: By Enitan Abdultawab Nigeria is preparing to bid to host the maiden edition of the Under-17 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON), as the country seeks to attract more international sporting competitions and strengthen its sports economy. The Director-General of the National Sports Commission (NSC), Bukola Olopade, disclosed this in a video shared on his X handle on Friday, saying Nigeria had already communicated its interest to the Confederation of African Football (CAF). According to Olopade, the country expressed its desire to host the competition during CAF’s General Assembly held in Abuja last weekend. “We have said to CAF that we are desirous of hosting the first Under-17 women’s championship,” he said. He explained that the move forms part of Nigeria’s ambition to move away from what he described as a consuming sports economy towards a productive one, where hosting international events would generate economic benefits for the country. “We don’t want to be a consuming sports economy; rather, we want to be a productive sports economy. We want to attract more international events where the economic impacts will be felt by the people,” Olopade added. CAF’s Executive Committee approved the introduction of the U-17 WAFCON on November 21, with the inaugural tournament scheduled to take place between March and April 2028. Qualifying matches are expected to begin in April 2027. Nigeria’s interest in hosting the competition comes amid discussions about the country’s readiness to stage major international football events. Earlier this week, FIFA President Gianni Infantino said Nigeria was not yet ready to host the men’s FIFA World Cup, although he acknowledged the country’s resources, passion and willingness to stage the competition. Infantino, however, suggested that Nigeria could demonstrate its organisational capacity by hosting smaller international football tournaments before taking on events of greater magnitude. The proposed U-17 WAFCON could therefore provide Nigeria with an opportunity to showcase its capacity to organise a continental football competition. The post Nigeria set to bid to host maiden U-17 WAFCON appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Hackers breach US Air Force Cloud computing platform
item.description: Hackers have breached Cloud One, the United States Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, potentially exposing sensitive military, personnel and logistics data. Three people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the intrusion was discovered within the past month during efforts to upgrade the system, triggering disruptions across the platform. However, the identity of the hackers, the full extent of the breach and whether any data was stolen remain unknown. In a statement to Reuters, the US Air Force declined to discuss the security status of specific networks and systems. It said: “We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities.” A major military computing platform Launched in 2017, Cloud One was designed as a centralised platform for the Air Force’s information technology needs, bringing together services provided by four major technology companies: Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet. The platform supports dozens of applications, including systems managing personnel records, salaries, logistics and military equipment maintenance. Among the applications hosted on Cloud One are the Air Force’s Cloud-Based Command and Control system, which consolidates air defence radar and other data feeds across North America, and the Theatre Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 US Air Force locations worldwide. Cloud One is regarded as one of the US military’s largest cloud computing platforms, according to two sources familiar with the matter. “A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources told Reuters. Investigators have reportedly involved US Cyber Command, the military’s cyber warfare arm, to assess the damage. Science Applications International Corporation (SAIC) served as the platform’s prime contractor until 2025, when Leidos took over the contract. SAIC did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment, while Leidos referred questions to the Air Force. Breach disrupts military operations The intrusion has reportedly triggered several disruptions across the platform. Two sources and another person familiar with the matter said plans to migrate additional back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, had been suspended. Updates to applications already running on the platform were also blocked, preventing Air Force personnel from installing fixes, even as new software vulnerabilities were being disclosed across the technology industry. Another source said some users had their administrator privileges revoked. One of the sources said the hackers exploited a software vulnerability to gain access to the platform’s control plane, which manages and oversees the underlying cloud infrastructure. The source likened the control plane to a universal remote, explaining that access could theoretically allow intruders to check the operational status of military aircraft or monitor the movement of spare

item.title: France slips into ‘technical recession’ after GDP revision
item.description: France’s economy has slipped into a technical recession after revised official figures showed that gross domestic product (GDP) contracted in the third quarter, extending the country’s economic decline. The National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE) said on Friday that the eurozone’s second-largest economy shrank by 0.2 per cent in the third quarter, revising its initial estimate of a 0.1 per cent contraction. The agency also revised second-quarter growth downwards to 0.02 per cent from zero per cent previously, although the figure was rounded to zero in the headline data. The revisions mean France’s economy has recorded consecutive quarterly contractions since the end of last year, meeting the conventional definition of a technical recession, which is two successive quarters of negative economic growth. The latest figures pose additional challenges for the government as it struggles to rein in the country’s budget deficit, with its target of 0.5 per cent economic growth this year now appearing increasingly difficult to achieve. The minority government is also facing difficulties securing parliamentary approval for its 2027 budget, which seeks to reduce the fiscal deficit from 5.4 per cent of GDP this year to five per cent next year. The budget debate comes five months before France’s presidential election, amid deep divisions in parliament. Reacting to the figures, Finance Minister Roland Lescure called for the speedy adoption of the budget, insisting that the five per cent deficit target was non-negotiable. “We must adopt a budget as soon as possible with a non-negotiable deficit target of 5%. It is imperative that we restore visibility for economic stakeholders,” he said. A breakdown of the third-quarter GDP figures by INSEE showed that weak domestic demand contributed to the contraction. Consumer spending rose by 0.3 per cent, but this was offset by a 0.8 per cent decline in business investment. The rebuilding of business inventories contributed 0.3 percentage points to GDP growth, following a 0.7 percentage-point reduction in the previous quarter. Foreign trade also weighed heavily on economic performance, subtracting 0.6 percentage points from output as exports fell by 1.6 per cent while imports increased by 0.1 per cent. Despite the contraction, the Bank of France said earlier in November that the economy was expected to record moderate growth in the fourth quarter. item.title: 10 Super Falcons players in camp ahead Algeria friendlies
item.description: A total of 10 Super Falcons players are currently in camp in Algeria ahead of their two international friendly matches against the host nation. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that four more players joined the team, bringing the number in camp to 10. The new arrivals are Shukurat Oladipo of AS Roma, Italy; Regina Otu of Fenerbahce Ladies, Turkey; Folashade Ijamilusi of Liaoning Shenyang, China; and Olamide Adugbe of Asteras Tripolis, Greece. The four players joined the initial six, comprising Christiana Uzoma and Valentina Uroko of Edo Queens, Glory Edet of Bayelsa Queens, Joy Igbokwe and Fatimoh Solaty of Nasarawa Amazons, and Blessing Nkor of Dynamo Brest, Belarus. The delegation is led by Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) Acting General Secretary Emmanuel Ikpeme and includes Interim Head Coach Augustine Eguavoen and members of his technical crew. More players are expected to join the camp later ahead of the team’s first training session. The Super Falcons will take on Algeria in two friendly matches on Monday and Dec. 4 as part of their international engagements. item.title: Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea
item.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration. Atmos and MBDA also said this work could lead to demonstrations, but the companies' announcement makes it clear that any deployment or use would be subject to the approval of governmental and military authorities. "The initiative also directly supports MBDA's broader strategic vision in the space domain, reinforcing both space for defense and the defense of space," Thomas Gottschild, MBDA Deutschland managing director, said in the same statement. This news comes a few months after Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said that the U.S. Space Force operates orbital weapons . "Let me be crystal clear: Today, Guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks," Schiess said during a conferenace presentation on Sept. 15 ("Guardians" refers to Space Force personnel.) Last year, Atmos' Phoenix capsule got its first test run in space. The cargo-return technology launched aboard a Space X Falcon 9 rocket during a rideshare mission in February 2025. Atmos tested out the inflatable heat shields it has been working on to help future space-manufactured cargo make it through Earth's atmosphere in one piece. "Orbital transportation and return form a new layer of strategic infrastructure, and infrastructure determines what Europe can achieve on its own terms," Klaus said in the Nov 18 statement.

item.title: Is Spain 'nostalgic' for Franco? Would traditional right PP consider an alliance with far-right Vox?
item.description: After eight years of socialist-led government, Spain is at a crossroads. Can Pedro Sánchez pull off another electoral comeback, or will the conservative Partido Popular make way for the far right into national government for the first time since the end of Franco's 40-year brutal reign? Just back from Madrid, Richard Werly, Europe correspondent for the Swiss daily Blick, joins Angela Diffley to examine the final days of campaigning and the generational divisions shaping Sunday’s snap elections. The youth are divided between the left and the far-right Vox party. Sánchez, nicknamed the “Teflon politician”, has campaigned heavily on housing and social issues. “We may see an outgoing prime minister performing better than expected,” says Werly.

item.title: 'From bad to catastrophic: Iran's justice system was already unfair for many decades'
item.description: Amid war with the US and Israel, Iranian protesters continue to face death sentences following what Amnesty International describes as grossly unfair, torture-tainted trials. “The situation has changed from bad to catastrophic,” says Raha Bahreini, Iranian-Canadian human rights lawyer and Amnesty International's researcher on Iran. Bahreini discusses the aftermath of the January 2026 protests, the authorities' efforts to equate peaceful dissent with treason and espionage, and the extrajudicial killings of peaceful protesters. Amnesty International is calling for an international criminal justice mechanism, potentially a special tribunal. “There needs to be criminal accountability for these crimes against humanity.”

item.title: Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension a Month After $6.3 Billion Hack
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension a Month After $6.3 Billion Hack Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it put in place after last month’s record $6.3 billion hack, saying its recovery work is complete and that withdrawals are open across nearly all networks. “Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted,” the exchange said in an X post Thursday afternoon. A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance, which Binance called standard practice and said was unrelated to the hack. The update closes out a month of phased reopenings. Binance confirmed the breach on Oct. 29, saying its initial investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave the attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals. The world’s largest crypto exchange stopped all customer withdrawals for two days after the theft, Reuters reported . When they first reopened, customers pulled a net $4.7 billion off the platform, Binance said on Nov. 2. Binance covered the losses Binance said on Nov. 12 that it had completed coverage of the affected assets with more than $6.34 billion of company funds. The money came from a partial draw on its Secure Asset Fund for Users, part of its futures insurance fund and its corporate treasury, and the exchange pledged to rebuild SAFU to about $1 billion. Coverage is not the same as recovery. Binance replaced the stolen tokens from its own books, while about $2.85 billion of the stolen funds have been frozen remotely by the companies that issue them. The rest remains in the hands of the attackers. U.S. authorities have blamed North Korean hackers for the theft, which North Korea denies. On Nov. 23, the Justice Department moved to forfeit more than $1.1 billion in USDC that Circle froze, and said the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion since the attack. Launderers turn to THORChain and coinjoin The unfrozen funds are on the move. North Korean launderers have stepped up transfers through THORChain and a coinjoin service in recent days, blockchain researchers told Reuters , as part of an operation spanning tens of thousands of transactions across blockchains. Chainalysis and Elliptic estimate that more than $600 million of the stolen crypto has passed through THORChain, though Elliptic said that figure could count funds that went through more than once. TRM Labs estimates THORChain earned as much as $1 million in fees from the swaps. Separately, $342 million has moved through a coinjoin service mostly coordinated by a pseudonymous figure named Kruw, Elliptic said. A coinjoin combines coins from many users into a single transaction, so their origin is no longer visible on the blockchain. Elliptic has said the launderers will still need other services, such as over-the-counter brokers, to turn the coins into cash. The FBI on Oct. 31 published

item.title: Osun LG Crisis Will Be Fully Resolved In The Next One Week — Gov Adeleke
item.description: Governor Ademola Adeleke has assured the people of Osun State that the protracted local government crisis in the state will be resolved within the next week, following President Bola Tinubu’s intervention. Governor Adeleke gave this assurance in his inaugural speech during his second-term inauguration held at Osogbo City Stadium, where he listed some of the priorities of his second-term administration across all sectors. “I am glad to announce that Mr President has intervened in the local government matter and in the next one week, the crisis will be fully resolved. Once this is done, our administration will ensure the rehabilitation of the remaining 102 primary health care centres,” he said. Osun Governor Ademola Adeleke was sworn in as governor for a second term on November 27, 2026. Photo: Femi Ojomo/Channels Television. As part of his priorities, the re-elected governor promised to set up the Osun State Electricity Regulatory Commission, as well as infrastructural expansion and recruitment of teachers and rehabilitation of schools, including reviving technical colleges. He also said that job and wealth creation will be at the heart of his second term. “We will establish a digital hub in each of our three senatorial districts. This is to drive job creation in the digital economy,” Adeleke said. “In education, we will recruit more teachers and speed up school rehabilitation. We will expand bursaries and scholarships, keep tuition affordable, tackle cultism, and revive our technical colleges.” In the health sector, he said about 70 per cent of existing primary health care centres were rehabilitated and equipped with solar and power facilities in his first term. “We upgraded and completed 232 out of 332 primary health care centres. The plan was to complete the whole 332 PHCs, but the seizure of local government allocations halted the process,” the governor said. “My government made sure that our primary school teachers, healthcare professionals at our primary healthcare centres, and local government retirees got paid in the last two years.” Osun Governor Ademola Adeleke sworn in as governor for a second term on November 27, 2026. Photo: Femi Ojomo/Channels Television. Adeleke said his vision is to move Osun from a civil service economy to an industrialised one, noting that his administration is open to partnership with private organisations and economic advisory groups. “Specifically, we will target agro-processing factories, industrial parks across districts, free trade zones, sports and tourism development, and a better business environment. “Fellow citizens, we must heal the wounds of the past and unite for our collective good. I charge the Osun political class to embrace elite consensus, transparency, good governance and local content,” he added. President Tinubu was represented at the inauguration by the Vice President, Kashim Shettima. item.title: Russia’s VTB Opens Bitcoin Trading as Central Bank Finalizes Crypto Test
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Russia’s VTB Opens Bitcoin Trading as Central Bank Finalizes Crypto Test Russian bank VTB began letting brokerage clients buy and sell bitcoin in its investing app on Friday, a day after the Bank of Russia approved the knowledge test every Russian crypto buyer now has to pass. Starting Nov. 27, clients of VTB’s brokerage can trade cryptocurrencies in the VTB My Investments app, the broker said . For now, the trades happen over the counter rather than on an exchange, and access is limited to qualified investors, the legal term for Russians who meet wealth or experience thresholds, who also pass the new test. “In our model, access to cryptocurrencies will require qualified investor status and passing special testing,” Andrei Yatskov, head of brokerage services at VTB, said . He said the test would appear in the app on Nov. 27 and work like the bank’s existing tests for other instruments. VTB handles the buying, storage and record-keeping itself on Russian infrastructure. To trade, clients need to open a separate digital account at VTB’s digital depository, where the crypto is held, on top of their regular brokerage account. The bank received its digital depository and crypto exchange licenses on Oct. 6. “At the start, we will focus on buying and selling cryptocurrencies, and then we will introduce additional services as regulation develops,” Yatskov said. Eight questions before the first trade The launch came quickly after the regulator moved. On Nov. 26, the Bank of Russia approved the first basic standards for brokers and crypto exchange offices, setting the rules for the test. Every investor has to take it, qualified or not, and it is free. Buyers must answer at least seven of eight questions correctly. The standard lays out eight topic blocks, from regulation, technical basics and information security to stablecoins, low-liquidity coins, address labeling and blocked transactions, and volatility, with one question drawn at random from each. Investors who fail can try once more the same day, with different questions. Brokers are barred from sharing the correct answers with clients or telling them which questions they missed. A passing result stays valid for one year from the test date or the latest trade, whichever comes later. The test was the missing piece for Russian banks. When retail buying became legal on Nov. 17 , T-Bank said it was waiting on a market standard for testing, and VTB said it was waiting on the remaining rules. Under the broker standard, the industry’s self-regulatory organization has three working days after publication to send brokers the answer options and correct answers. Ordinary investors still face tight limits once they pass. Non-qualified buyers can only purchase bitcoin, ether and Tether’s USDT, and no more than 300,000 rubles a year through a single intermediary. SPB Exchange sets Dec. 1 start Exchange trading is next. SPB Exchange said Friday it will open spot trading in bitcoin, ether and USDT ag

item.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
item.description: null Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone. The five stars are still there, but the shape you may have memorized looks like it's been picked up and turned over. It looks more like an E or an M, depending on when you look. Now try and look for the Big Dipper /the Plough. It's gone. Nothing mysterious has happened, of course. Cassiopeia is doing exactly what it always does, but it's a reminder that the northern sky is where you can easily watch the stars move — and the seasons turn. What's happening and when to look Stars move anti-clockwise around the north celestial pole, so Cassiopeia changes orientation. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) Late November is an excellent time to reacquaint yourself with Cassiopeia from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Look high in the northern sky during the evening for its five prominent stars — Caph, Schedar, Navi, Ruchbah and Segin. Depending on exactly when you look, it can look like a W, E, M or a 3. This is because Cassiopeia is circumpolar. Rather than rising in the east and eventually setting in the west like many familiar constellations , it circles the north celestial pole — a position currently held by Polaris , the North Star. From sufficiently northerly latitudes, its main stars never disappear below the horizon. This gives us a simple observing experiment. Find Cassiopeia in the early evening and remember its orientation relative to the horizon. Go back several hours later and look again. The constellation has moved around Polaris, and its shape has changed. The stars haven't changed their arrangement — Earth has simply rotated from west to east. We all know this logically, but watching the familiar pattern of Cassiopeia's stars apparently tip over during a single night makes Earth's rotation a lot less abstract. How and when I'm watching it The names and distances of the stars in Cassiopeia. (Image credit: Starry Night) I'm going to observe Cassiopeia twice on the same evening this week, which is about as complicated as the experiment needs to get. The first time will be shortly after darkness falls. I'll find the W, note which way it seems to be pointing and use something fixed — a rooftop, tree or chimney — to give myself a rough reference for its position. I'll return to my backyard before bed, and see where the pattern ha

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
item.description: null On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting. (Image credit: Alto Vintage Images/Alamy) Why it mattered Not many stargazers may be be acquainted with the Andromedid meteor shower. What used to be a spectacular annual meteor shower is now hardly even visible. But in 1885, the Andromedids were an annual treat for skywatchers hoping for a chance to see the remains of Biela's comet (a comet first spotted in 1772 and then found - for the third time - in 1826 by the German astronomer Wilhelm von Biela, from whom it gets its name). Meteor Shower Quiz: How Well Do You Know 'Shooting Stars'? This modern photo of the Geminid meteor shower shows dozens of meteors captured in a long exposure by Josh Drury. Ladislaus Weinek, who captured the first photo of a meteor, had to use a photographic plate in 1889. (Image credit: Josh Dury) Camera technology has come a long way since 1885, which is good since it is a bit harder to see the Andromedids these days. Instead of photographic plates or digital cameras, astronomers now have to use special tracking equipment to record images of Andromedid meteors. In 2011, astronomers announced that the meteor shower seemed to be undergoing a resurgence of activity, with 50 meteors per hour, and upticks were expected in 2018 and 2023. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: New York Wins $1.37 Billion Judgment Against NovaTech Crypto Ponzi Founders
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine New York Wins $1.37 Billion Judgment Against NovaTech Crypto Ponzi Founders A New York judge has ordered the founders of NovaTech, a cryptocurrency investment scheme that targeted Haitian communities, to pay more than $1.37 billion, closing out the state’s case against a couple who fled the country rather than answer it. Justice Anar Rathod Patel of the New York County Supreme Court signed the order on Nov. 24. It holds Cynthia and Eddy Petion and their companies NovaTech Ltd, NovaTech Advisors and NovaPay jointly liable for $1,367,023,585 in disgorgement and interest. New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the win on Wednesday. “Today’s historic judgment finally delivers some semblance of justice for the thousands of New Yorkers who were targeted by this merciless scam,” James said. “NovaTech cruelly targeted immigrant families through faith and community groups with the promise of a better life while robbing them of their life savings.” Where the $1.37 billion figure comes from The award matches what the attorney general’s office asked for in October . The figure starts with the cryptocurrency investors sent to NovaTech’s wallet at payment processor CoinPayments, which totaled about $1.16 billion from August 2019 through May 2023, according to an affirmation filed by the state. Prosecutors subtracted the roughly $26 million NovaTech actually moved to its trading platform, leaving $1.13 billion in principal. Nine percent annual interest from June 2023 through September 2025 added another $232.5 million. NovaTech’s traders lost about $18.2 million of the money they did trade, the filing said. Everything else paid out of the wallet, including so-called returns and recruitment bonuses, came from other investors’ deposits. Cynthia Petion was the only authorized user on the CoinPayments account, and the state says she approved at least $134.5 million in crypto withdrawals to wallets belonging to her and her husband. The judge also ordered the Petions’ earlier venture, AWS Mining, to pay about $1.46 million. Cynthia Petion owes a separate $4.69 million tied to her promotion of that scheme. A NovaTech scheme built on prayer groups AWS Mining sold crypto mining contracts and promised 15% to 20% monthly returns before it collapsed in 2019, according to the attorney general’s office. The Petions then launched NovaTech, falsely marketed it as a registered hedge fund broker and advertised trading profits of about 2% to 4% a week. Promoters recruited through prayer groups, WhatsApp chats and ads in Haitian Creole. More than 11,000 New Yorkers invested, alongside what the state called hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide. NovaTech collapsed in May 2023, and tens of thousands of investors couldn’t withdraw their crypto. The state sued in June 2024. The Petions never answered the complaint. The court entered a default judgment in August 2025 that found they violated New York’s Martin Act and banned them from the securities, c

item.title: Smartphone shipments face another bleak year before modest 2028 comeback
item.description: Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028. That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker , which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers. The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market. Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns. The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC , memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing. As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones. Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported , memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026. For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases. "The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang. "Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets." Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years. Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing. A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery. "The unusually low 2027 base creates the potential for a robust rebound in 2028 once the memory bottleneck begins to ease. But this should not b

item.title: Artemis III astronauts meet their spacecraft | Space photo of the day for Nov. 27, 2026
item.description: null NASA's Artemis III astronauts pose holding up three fingers to symbolize their mission as they visit the Orion spacecraft they will ride to space. (Image credit: NASA/Kim Shiflett) Training for a mission to space is hard work. But sometimes you have to take a minute and have a little fun with your crewmates. What is it? Crowded together with the Orion spacecraft, the four astronauts that make up the Artemis III crew hold up three fingers, taking a brief pause in their rigorous training for some lighthearted crew bonding. In the snapshot , the crew — from left to right, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick (mission commander) and Frank Rubio (mission specialist), European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano (mission pilot) and NASA astronaut Andre Douglas (mission specialist) — is spotted posing alongside the same Orion spacecraft that they will fly to space as part of their mission. This brief moment of levity took place where the spacecraft currently resides at the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Why is it incredible? This crew has a serious mission ahead of them. The four astronauts will launch to low-Earth orbit around Earth where they plan to practice rendezvous and docking with both Blue Origin and SpaceX's lunar landing vehicles , Blue Moon and Starship, respectively. To prepare, the crew has to undergo months of critical training to both be physically ready while prepared to handle any situation that might come up during their mission. And while Artemis III isn't landing astronauts on the moon, it is a critical step toward that goal. If Artemis III goes to plan and NASA has a lunar landing vehicle that passes rendezvous and docking tests with the Orion spacecraft, Artemis IV might see astronauts land on the moon for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

item.title: NASA’s NG-25 Mission to Launch Pioneering Space Crops Research
item.description: Experiments in the Ohalo III facility (pictured above) aim to validate plant-water delivery, optimize volume, and advance crop-production research. These insights could inform the design of plant production systems for future deep-space missions. NASA NASA experiments, including a first-of-its-kind space crop production system, will travel to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 25th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency. Investigations from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division will advance research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration, expanding knowledge of space crops and human health. Groundbreaking space crops Astronauts will need sustainable sources of food to travel farther and stay longer in space. To help understand how crop production works in microgravity, NASA is launching a novel space crops experiment . The new prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing safe, nutritious, and reliable crop production systems for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions. Knowledge gained from the space crop production system also could help inform agricultural practices such as vertical farming and indoor growing systems. Researchers will use this investigation to validate the system’s water delivery and volume optimization technology aboard the space station. Tiny brain models aboard station A precision health investigation is the next step toward enabling long-duration studies of human brain tissues in space. The research builds on a previous investigation that sent small, lab-grown models of the human brain, called miBrains, to the space station. This experiment will validate a miniature fluid-handling system designed to mix, deliver, and maintain the nutrient-rich liquid needed to keep the tissues alive. Researchers could use the findings to help identify potential neurological risks associated with spaceflight and develop strategies to protect astronaut health. It also may advance human tissue research and neurological disease modeling on Earth. Biological & Physical Sciences Division NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

item.title: Bill for Birmingham's Oracle debacle reaches £128M
item.description: Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse. Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF]. The report , from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million. The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues. "The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said. It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software. The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems. Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts . It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor . The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt , an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system. It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless. The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay , now rebranded as Civica Income Management. Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill. For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools , but that was excluded from the reimplementation. Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example. A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026. item.title: Bitcoin Price Trades Near $61,300 as Tech Stock Futures Rally
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Trades Near $61,300 as Tech Stock Futures Rally The bitcoin price traded near $61,300 on Friday morning, as tech stock futures jumped ahead of a holiday-shortened session on Wall Street. Bitcoin price is on track for its first weekly gain after seven straight weekly losses, though it is still down about 20% in November. The bitcoin price was up about 1.7% early Friday and set to add 4.8% for the week, Investing.com reported , extending a recovery from a two-year low of $57,325.70 hit earlier in the week. Bitcoin slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday as the Nasdaq sank at the open, before a late rebound in tech shares lifted risk assets. Short sellers helped fuel the bounce. Shorts made up 77% of $84.7 million in bitcoin liquidations over the past day, while futures open interest was little changed. That suggests forced short covering, rather than fresh leverage, supplied much of the lift. Tech futures lead the risk rebound Nasdaq 100 futures rose 2.2% by 6:42 a.m. ET, Reuters reported, as investors returned from Thanksgiving and piled back into battered AI-linked shares. Nvidia gained 3.6% in premarket trading, while AMD climbed 4.4% and Broadcom added 3.4%. S&P 500 futures rose 1.6%, and Dow futures gained 1.3%. “There have been some signs that the tech selloff has stabilised for now, and that risk appetite is returning to markets,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note cited by Reuters. The S&P 500 is headed for its best week since April, though it remains on course for its worst November since 2008. Bitcoin price has followed that rebound but lagged it. The major U.S. stock indexes are each up around 4% on the week, and silver jumped about 7% to above $44 an ounce on Friday while gold added 2.5% to above $3,670. Stocks close early at 1 p.m. ET, and the bond market shuts at 2 p.m. Rate hike bets and ETF outflows linger The macro backdrop still weighs on the bitcoin price. Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike in December after data this week showed the economy grew faster than first estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated in October, Reuters reported. Third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 4.3%, and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.84%. Spot bitcoin ETFs are also still losing cash. The U.S. funds lost $453 million on Wednesday, their seventh straight day of outflows, with BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounting for $329.7 million. That pushed November outflows to about $5.39 billion, extending what was already a record month for the funds. Crypto stocks and miners in focus Crypto stocks face their own test in Friday’s short session. Strategy shares rose 3.1% to $79.96 on Wednesday, while Coinbase gained 1.3% to $103.72. Bitcoin miners that have moved into AI hosting tracked the tech rally, with IREN and Cipher Digital each gaining 8% in premarket trading. item.title: Galaxy Withdraws Call That Bitcoin’s Bear Market Ended in June
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Galaxy Withdraws Call That Bitcoin’s Bear Market Ended in June Galaxy has withdrawn its October call that bitcoin’s bear market ended in June, saying the technical signal behind it failed after seven straight weeks of losses and that the bear market is “very likely not over.” Alex Thorn, Galaxy’s head of firmwide research, laid out the reversal in a report published Wednesday and sent to clients a day earlier. “We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June,” the report said. “The signal it rested on has failed.” The firm’s Oct. 26 note had argued that bitcoin had entered an accumulation phase. Galaxy said at the time that a weekly close back below the 50-week moving average that was not regained within a month would invalidate its technical case. That is what happened. Bitcoin closed the week ended Nov. 8 at $74,968, 0.7% below the 50-week average, after seven weekly closes above it. It then closed the week ended Nov. 15 below the 200-week average, which Galaxy has described as the floor of past bear markets. Galaxy points to $58,525 The week ended Nov. 22 closed at $61,104, 17.9% below the 50-week average and 10.4% below the 200-week average of $68,159. Bitcoin traded below its July 1 intraday low on Nov. 20 and reached $55,100 on Nov. 21, but the June 30 closing low of $58,525 held on a daily basis through Nov. 22. Galaxy now treats that level as the line to watch. A daily close below $58,525 would be “the start of a move to a materially lower low,” the report said, and the firm would not treat such a close as a buying signal by itself. History is not kind to breaks like that. In the seven prior bear market cases where bitcoin closed below a low that had stood for at least 60 days, the eventual low was at least 17% lower, with a median of 52%. Applied to the June low, that works out to about $48,500 and $28,200. Bitcoin briefly slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday morning as the Nasdaq sank, but it ended the day back above $60,000 and has not posted a daily close below $58,525. It traded near $60,800 on Thursday morning. Late by the clock, early by the depth Galaxy said two readings of the market disagree. By the calendar, this bear is old: Nov. 22 was day 412 since the Oct. 6, 2025, record, longer than the 163 to 406 days from high to low in the four prior bear markets. By depth, it looks unfinished. Bitcoin’s 53% decline compares with drops of 77% to 93% in earlier bears. It also has not closed a day below its realized price of $53,205, something every prior bear did for at least 140 days, and only two of the 13 bottom signals Galaxy tracks have been met. “The clock says this bear is overdue to end, the depth says it has further to fall, and we do not believe the price record alone can settle which,” the report said. Flows have not helped. Galaxy estimates U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs hold about 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below their October 2025 peak, after shedding 71,339 BTC, or $4.95 billion, since Oct. 4. item.title: UK government rejects national consultation on AI datacenters
item.description: The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures. Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed. The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared. In its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027. "Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) says. "Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI." But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests. This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance. The government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning. Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources. If this has a ring of familiarity, it is because President Trump earlier this year introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge , under which hyperscalers and AI companies agreed to protect US consumers from any bill shocks due to the energy and infrastructure requirements of their datacenter projects. It seems that where the US leads, the UK still often follows. The Covenant sets out efficiency targets and reporting expectations, but does not explain how compliance will be enforced or specify penalties for failing to meet its tests. Protect the

item.title: Lloyds and Bank of Scotland apps fall over on payday
item.description: Lloyds Bank and Bank of Scotland customers reported problems accessing online banking and transferring money on Friday morning. Reports on Downdetector began rising around 1000 UTC. Lloyds also acknowledged problems on its service status page . A reader who supplied the screenshot below noted the particularly awkward timing: the last Friday of the month is payday for many workers. It's also retail silly season: while Brits don't celebrate Thanksgiving, many UK outlets nonetheless participate in Black Friday sales, meaning storefronts are losing out. Others are concerned with more practical purchases. One customer tweeted that she had "no food at home and cannot shop because I cannot transfer funds from my secondary Lloyds account to my main one. At this point I'm just going to withdraw every penny the moment I'm paid, so much for Internet banking. Never had this years ago." Bank of Scotland, another Lloyds Banking Group brand, reported similar problems on its service status page : " We're aware some customers are having issues with our app and online banking at the moment. We're sorry about this and are working hard to fix it." Earlier this year, a botched overnight software update at Lloyds Banking Group potentially exposed other customers' transaction information to almost 448,000 app users. In a letter to Parliament's Treasury Committee, consumer relationships CEO Jasjyot Singh blamed a defect in the API handling transaction data. The incident affected Lloyds, Halifax, and Bank of Scotland, and prompted goodwill payments to thousands of customers. Lloyds Banking Group said late last year that it had more than 21 million mobile app users and over 23 million digitally active customers. A spokesperson for Lloyds Banking Group told The Register : "We're aware some customers are having difficulty accessing the app this morning. We’re sorry for the inconvenience and are working to get things back to normal as quickly as possible." ®

item.title: Europe's AI sovereignty push: Lots of cloud, not much silver lining
item.description: Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles. Gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion. For 2026, it estimates spending growth of 20.7 percent in North America and 13.7 percent in China. "The world seems to be racing towards this AI goal of where the large language model provider is going to be, and the race seems to be between North American-based providers and some Asia Pacific providers," John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, told The Register . He said Europe had traditionally trailed in IT uptake. "We saw that happen when global sourcing, cloud, and software as a service all came along. It's down to the pushback against the idea of creative destruction," where new technologies replace old ones. Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent. Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment. "For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he said. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use." The gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced new rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much. "Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign. "They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their company in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us. Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach. "The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," said Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®

item.title: Israel Olaleye: How Can Young Nigerians Buy Land & Properties Legitimately Today?
item.description: Young man with a hard hat holding a red for sale sign outside a building by Pavel Danilyuk for Pexels . My parents’ generation mostly bought land the way their parents did. Someone in the family knew someone in the village. An uncle walked the boundaries. The community remembered who owned what, and if anything went wrong, you had a face to go back to. However, my generation buys land on Instagram. I do not say that to mock anyone. I sell land for a living. When I started in real estate sales in 2023, two years after finishing a Mathematics degree at the University of Ibadan, I assumed buyers would care most about price and location. They do care. But what I hear most often is fear, dressed up as questions. Can I trust you? Is this land real? What happens if I miss a payment? After I pay, will someone come and ask me for more money? A prospective buyer once asked me, before anything else, whether community or family payments would follow after she paid for her plot. She was not asking about the land. She was asking whether the price I quoted was the real price. She had good reason to ask. Lagos State’s Property Protection Law of 2016 made it an offence to demand levies for construction on someone else’s property. Yet the same law still allows a land-owning family, with the family head’s authority, to collect a customary fee for possession, the payment many people know as a “foundation levy”. So the honest answer to her question is not a simple yes or no. It depends on the land, the family, and what has been written down. Most first-time buyers have never been told any of this. That is the gap I keep coming back to. Nobody taught us how to buy land. We learned how to save. Some of us learned how to invest in stocks, crypto or a side business. But land, the asset our parents spoke about with the most respect, has no manual. The people who used to stand in for the manual–the uncle, the community, the family lawyer everyone trusted–are often not part of how we buy anymore. So we improvise. A prospect once told me she had gone through my Instagram page carefully before she agreed to speak with me. She was checking whether I was consistent, whether my posts matched what I said on the phone, whether I had been around long enough to be real. I was flattered. Then I was worried. Because if a social media page has become part of a buyer’s due diligence, then a polished page has also become one of the easiest ways to deceive her. Instagram cannot tell you who owns a piece of land. Only a search at the land registry, done by your own lawyer, can begin to tell you that. Instagram cannot tell you whether a plot sits under government acquisition or on a planned road. A surveyor who charts the coordinates and checks them against official maps can. No number of testimonials replaces a written contract that states what you are paying for, what you are not paying for, and what happens if a payment is missed. None of this is complicated. It is just not taught. The i

item.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
item.description: null Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." item.title: AI boom leaves network operators waiting up to 18 months for kit
item.description: The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN. RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components. As Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN says optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months. This is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders . The issue now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies. In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN says developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening. The sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN says. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the issue. However, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time. Network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report says. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now. The aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly. RETN also says AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available. Remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this issue earlier this year. For sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site. item.title: British social security system techies yank services offline following 'cyber incident'
item.description: The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has taken some services offline after detecting a "cyber incident," but says regular benefit and pension payments are unaffected. The department announced the precautionary shutdown on Friday morning. "We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems," it said. "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimize any disruption. "Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links." The Register contacted both the DWP and NCSC for more information. The DWP declined to comment beyond the statement issued publicly. GC3 coordinates responses to incidents affecting government. The Government Cyber Unit leads the wider Government Cyber Action Plan, backed by more than £210 million. It is led by the government CISO, Bella Powell. Officials have not commented on any of the usual details one would expect from a cyber incident disclosure, including the specific services that were downed, when they are expected to return, or whether any data is thought to be compromised, even at this early stage. The UK government has also been criticized recently for investing heavily in AI cyber defenses, while the issue of legacy and aging IT continues to be neglected in the background. It announced at the end of October that it was throwing £130 million at AI cyber defense technology , as part of a wider £600 million cross-government AI spending spree announced by the Treasury. ExfilSquad recently claimed to have stolen around 607,000 records from the Department for Education and another 114,000 from the Police National Legal Database. ®

item.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
item.description: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick? For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce. Advertisement If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet , money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world. The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia , the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X , part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. In it, the recipe suggests using the “urine of a small child”, although today our understanding of the chemical reaction tha

item.title: Read an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman
item.description: The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy in December “ A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder. Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child. Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood. Advertisement Decant this properly, and use. ” Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X , c. 300 CE In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements. For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it. The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When d’Anastasy wasn’t trading – or rescuing enslaved girls during the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire – he ran a side-hustle, “procuring” relics from Ancient Egypt and selling them to the salons of Europe: statues to the British Museum in London; rings and jewels to the Louvre in Paris; even a pair of sphinxes that still sit on the banks of the Neva River in St Petersburg. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands. Among the Leiden trove was one of the most remarkable finds in history: a papyrus scroll with a list of recipes, each with crystal-clear instructions written in Greek. While we have damaged cuneiform tablets and later copies of older works, the Leiden Papyrus X , written around 300 CE, is the oldest surviving alchemy book in history. It is a guide for Egyptian artisans to create wondrous riches, seemingly out of nothing. There are methods on how to polish silverware, cheap alternatives for making knock-off purple robes, and how to create gold lettering by mixing saffron and tortoise bile. These are all real instructions, and all recipes that work (even if, today, there are cheaper ways to get the same result). Among them is the greatest secret in alchemy. It’s called the “invention

item.title: Royal Navy orders £142M in minehunting drones from US supplier
item.description: Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) says that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs). These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a " Hybrid Navy " comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges. The UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620 , built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding company in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company. We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry. The contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII says it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting. HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations. The new vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open. By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class , but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems. The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP , an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance. The new REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD. "This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP. Like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy. In trials announced in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®
